newsitem.title: CHINA: Russia PM China visit to forge into trade territory.
newsitem.headline: Russia PM China visit to forge into trade territory.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's trip to China is aimed at following up revived Sino-Russian political relations with equal progress on the economic front, diplomats said on Wednesday.

Chernomyrdin arrives in Beijing on Thursday for a three-day visit spearheaded by an advance force of trade and energy officials who have been busy forging huge deals for the prime minister to sign, said one Russian diplomat in Beijing.
"This is a kind of turning point now because both sides have come to the point that they should sign some agreements in the economic sphere," the diplomat said.
"All these years there has been a lack of substantial economic co-operation and investment in science and technology," the diplomat said.
Sino-Russian ties have gradually thawed since 1989 when the two sides formally mended relations after years of bitter struggles over territorial disputes and leadership of the socialist world.

The euphoric warming in political relations was capped last April when presidents Jiang Zemin and Boris Yeltsin met in Moscow and signed a joint declaration outlining the two nations' vision of the post-Cold War world order.
"The boosting of political ties will help expand the economic co-operation," the Russian diplomat said.

Among the deals Chernomyrdin and his Chinese counterpart Li Peng were expected to sign was a multi-billion dollar project to exploit Siberian natural gas to meet China's growing demand for energy, other diplomats said.

Chinese and Russian officials, including Minister of Nuclear Energy Viktor Mikailov, would also discuss the progress of work on a multi-billion nuclear power plant in China's eastern province of Jiangsu, the diplomat said. He did not give details.
China once was a net oil exporter, but speedy economic growth has fuelled demand for energy, with Chinese officials predicting oil imports could reach an annual 50 million tonnes by 2000.

"Both sides have stressed...that the goal of achieving $20 billion in trade by 2000 must be implemented, first of all by means of expanded investment and industrial co-operation," the Russian diplomat said.

Trade between China and Russia was about $6.8 billion last year, with a surplus of about $3.0 billion in Russia's favour, Russian officials said. Beijing estimates total trade could reach $8-10 billion in 1997.
Chernomyrdin was due to spend Thursday in Shenzhen near the border with Hong Kong before flying to Beijing for meetings on Friday with Li. The two met in Moscow last December.
They would stamp their seals on a railroad pact aimed at greasing the wheels of trade.
"These deals will be quite important and will have a value of many billions of U.S. dollars," the Russian diplomat said. He declined to give their exact worth.

Both Beijing and Moscow wanted to try to spur growth in large investment projects rather than simply increase trade in common consumer goods and raw materials that made up much of Sino-Russian trade, he said.
"Both sides are vigorously trying to create some additional incentives for the big companies on both sides to go to the Russian market, to go to the Chinese market," he said.

Among other energy-related deals, a Russian consortium is vying for a contract to supply China with 14 generators with a total installed capacity of 9,800 megawatts for the gargantuan Three Gorges dam on the Yangtze River.
